claims.summary: The retrieved evidence gives no TcB schedule for preterm infants: the NICHD ELBW trial measured bilirubin at least once daily for the first 7 days and then conditionally in the second week, a 2026 preterm graphing paper extends decision support to at least 14 days, and NICE recommends serum rather than transcutaneous measurement below 35 weeks [Morris2008; Stavis2026; NICE2023].

evidence.quote: Bilirubin was measured at least once daily for the first 7 days after birth for all infants. During the second week after birth, bilirubin was measured on any day on which phototherapy was administered or when phototherapy had been stopped in the previous 24 hours or the last bilirubin measurement exceeded 5 mg per deciliter for infants with a birth weight of 501 to 750 g or 7 mg per deciliter for infants with a birth weight 751 to 1000 g.

Chronologic age-based guidelines based on gestational age (GA) at birth were derived from the consensus-based recommendations and modified with integration of the AAP hyperbilirubinemia guidelines and extension of decision support for a minimum of 14 days.
Use serum bilirubin measurement for babies: in the first 24 hours of life or who have a gestational age of less than 35 weeks. [2016]

claims.summary: Systematic reviews and a California multicentre study of infants <30 weeks support TcB as a screening test in preterm infants, with serum confirmation of positive results and more careful use below 33 weeks as TcB approaches treatment thresholds, whereas NICE recommends serum measurement below 35 weeks, and the only retrieved TcB-to-serum rule (TSB when TcB exceeds or is within 3 mg/dL of the phototherapy threshold, or is ≥15 mg/dL) comes from the AAP guideline for infants ≥35 weeks [Nagar2013; Okwundu2023; Sankar2023; Jegathesan2021; NICE2023; Kemper2022].

evidence.quote: Pooled estimates in infants <32 weeks' gestation were similar to the overall preterm population (r = 0.89 [95% confidence interval: 0.82-0.93]).
The TcB devices reliably estimated bilirubin levels in preterm infants and could be used in clinical practice to reduce blood sampling.

The high sensitivity of TcB to detect hyperbilirubinaemia suggests that TcB devices are reliable screening tests for ruling out hyperbilirubinaemia in newborn infants. Positive test results would require confirmation through serum bilirubin measurement.
Our study supports the use of TcB as a screening tool for monitoring jaundice in extremely preterm infants.

Among preterm infants, TcB may offer a noninvasive, immediate approach to screening for hyperbilirubinemia with more careful use in preterm infants born at <33 weeks' gestation, as TcB approaches treatment thresholds.
Use serum bilirubin measurement for babies: in the first 24 hours of life or who have a gestational age of less than 35 weeks. [2016]

claims.summary: The 2022 AAP guideline, which replaces the 2004 guideline, no longer uses the Bhutani risk-zone nomogram and instead measures TSB when TcB exceeds or is within 3 mg/dL of the gestational-age- and risk-factor-specific phototherapy threshold or is ≥15 mg/dL [Kemper2022].
claims.note: Current evidence suggests that for infants ≥35 weeks the decision to measure TSB rests on the distance between the TcB and the phototherapy threshold for the infant's gestational age and neurotoxicity risk factors (TcB exceeding or within 3 mg/dL of it) or a TcB ≥15 mg/dL [Kemper2022]. The 2022 AAP guideline describes the earlier risk nomogram, based on the 1999 Bhutani study, as not accounting for gestational age or neurotoxicity risk factors and as derived from a population that excluded DAT-positive infants, and the nomogram study defined its high-risk zone by TSB percentiles in healthy, mostly term newborns [Kemper2022; Bhutani1999].

claims.manual_text: Additional TCB screening for DAT+: DAT+ and GA ≥ 32wks --> Check TCB at 6 hrs; If TCB <4, continue regular screening; If TCB 4-5, repeat TCB at 12 hrs; If TCB ≥ 5, draw TSB. Notify MD if TSB > 5 (repeat TCB at 12 hrs --> If TCB ≥ 5, draw TSB)
claims.summary: In ABO-incompatible DAT-positive newborns ≥35 weeks, a sixth-hour TcB was highly predictive of phototherapy within 24 hours, with a low-risk cut-off of <3.0 mg/dL and a high-risk cut-off of ≥5.3 mg/dL, and the AAP guideline lists isoimmune hemolytic disease as a neurotoxicity risk factor, while NICE recommends serum measurement in the first 24 hours and below 35 weeks [Papacostas2022; Kemper2022; NICE2023].
claims.note: Current evidence suggests a sixth-hour TcB is highly predictive of the need for phototherapy within 24 hours in ABO-incompatible DAT-positive newborns, in a retrospective study limited to infants ≥35 weeks that reported a low-risk cut-off of <3.0 mg/dL (negative predictive value 98%) and a high-risk cut-off of ≥5.3 mg/dL (positive predictive value 85%) [Papacostas2022]. The AAP guideline treats isoimmune hemolytic disease (positive DAT) as a hyperbilirubinemia neurotoxicity risk factor and covers infants ≥35 weeks, while NICE recommends serum rather than transcutaneous measurement in the first 24 hours of life and below 35 weeks [Kemper2022; NICE2023].

evidence.quote: Of 10 942 consecutive newborns ≥35 weeks estimated gestational age, 829 were ABO incompatible and DAT positive.
Low (<3.0 mg/dL) and high (≥5.3 mg/dL) risk TcB cutoffs demonstrated a negative predictive value of 98% and positive predictive value of 85%, respectively.
Among high-risk ABO incompatible DAT positive newborns, the sixth-hour TcB is highly predictive of the need for phototherapy ≤24 hours.

Based on these results, we have insufficient confidence in the effect estimate for benefit of IVIg to make even a weak recommendation for the use of IVIg for the treatment of alloimmune HDN.
